resources.string: Measure each ear and even out the sound of the whole device

A short listening test measures how sensitive each ear is at six frequencies. From that, the device builds a separate equaliser curve per ear and applies it to media in any app: music, videos, podcasts.\n\nNotification, alarm and ringtone sounds keep their usual sound, and phone calls are not affected: call audio goes straight from the modem to the earpiece.
Put on headphones and run the check.
Both ears measured evenly. No correction needed.
Correcting a %1$d dB spread. Your %2$s ear at %3$s is the weakest point.
Nothing is being corrected. Your %1$s ear at %2$s is the weakest point; turn the correction on to even out the rest against it.
At this strength the correction stays under 1 dB, so you won\'t hear a difference. Raise it to even out your %1$s ear at %2$s.
Shapes every sound the mixer plays, not just one app. While it is on, compressed audio is decoded in software rather than offloaded to the DSP, which costs a little battery during long playback.
100% corrects half of the measured difference, which is the standard fitting rule. Lower is gentler.
The correction works by holding back the frequencies you hear best, so it makes things quieter. This wins some of that back; a limiter stops it clipping.
The measurement and the curve built from it are removed, and the correction is turned off. You can run the check again at any time.

Put on headphones — the two ears are tested separately, so loudspeakers cannot be used.\n\nFind somewhere quiet. Background noise masks the quiet tones and will make your hearing look worse than it is.

Play the reference tone and use the volume keys until it is clearly audible but comfortable. Everything in the test is measured against this level, and no tone will ever be louder than 15 dB above it.\n\nOnce the test starts, leave the volume alone.
Connect headphones to start. The test can\'t run on the phone\'s speaker.
Headphones disconnected, so the test stopped. Nothing was saved.

Press the button every time you hear a tone, however faint — if you think you might have heard something, press.\n\nSome of the tones are very quiet and some are silent on purpose. Long gaps are normal.

Higher is better: the higher a point, the quieter the tone you could still hear. Blue crosses are your left ear, red circles your right. The scale is in dB against the level you set as comfortable (0), not clinical dB HL. Nothing here is calibrated equipment.

How each ear will be equalised. The curve only pulls bands down, never up. Applying it also adds back some overall loudness (make-up gain, adjustable later on the home screen), with a limiter to stop that from clipping.
Your thresholds span %1$d dB, with %2$s the hardest for you to hear.
Your ears differ by %1$d dB at %2$s. That gap is what pulls the stereo image off centre, and it is what the per-ear correction fixes.
The media volume changed during the test, so the thresholds are measured against two different levels. Worth running again.
You answered %1$d of %2$d silent trials. Enough of those means the results read better than your hearing really is — worth running again, pressing only when you are fairly sure.
